name: Fluocinonide

card.summary: A potent prescription topical corticosteroid that calms inflamed, itchy skin and scalp conditions such as eczema, psoriasis and patchy alopecia areata so skin looks clearer and hair can regrow.
card.note: Prescription-only potent steroid; prolonged use can thin the skin.

quick.overview:
Fluocinonide is a potent glucocorticoid applied to the skin as cream, ointment, gel or solution. Wikipedia lists its use for skin disorders such as eczema and seborrhoeic dermatitis, where it relieves itching, redness, dryness, scaling and inflammation.[1]

For appearance, the payoff is calmer, less red and flaky skin. Dermatologists also use topical steroids for patchy hair loss: a case series of congenital alopecia areata lists fluocinonide among the steroids used,[4] and some forum users report using it for beard or scalp patches, with mixed experiences.[13][14]
quick.how: It is a prescription product applied to affected patches in thin layers under a clinician's direction, usually for limited periods. It is sometimes paired with other treatments, such as tacrolimus in one forum account of beard alopecia areata, or tazarotene in psoriasis comparisons.[14][5]
quick.risks: Skin atrophy (thinning) is the commonly described adverse effect of potent topical steroids.[1] Fluocinonide is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia.[1] One forum user reports flares after stopping it,[13] and a 1983 trial letter examined tachyphylaxis, a loss of response over time.[8]

lead: Fluocinonide is a high-potency topical corticosteroid prescribed for inflammatory skin conditions. Wikipedia reports brand names including Lidex and Fluonex, a prescription-only status in the US, UK and Australia, and over a million US prescriptions in 2022.[1]

In dermatology it has been used for eczema, psoriasis, oral lichen planus and discoid lupus, among others.[2][3][7] A 2025 randomized trial in 47 people with oral lichen planus found fluocinonide 0.05% gel reduced symptoms, signs and lesion extension over six months compared with placebo.[6]

Appearance-related interest centers on inflamed skin and patchy hair loss. Case reports of alopecia areata describe topical steroids including fluocinonide,[4] and community members describe being prescribed it for alopecia barbae and other patches.[13][14]

angle.goal: Clearer skin / hair regrowth in patches
chain: Skin looks calmer; hair may regrow in autoimmune patches
angle.text: By lowering inflammation, it makes affected skin look less red and flaky and is one of the topical steroids used in patchy alopecia areata.

paras: Wikipedia lists eczema and seborrhoeic dermatitis, noting relief of itching, redness, dryness, crusting and scaling.[1] Trials compared fluocinonide with betamethasone valerate in older studies,[10][11] used it alongside phototherapy in psoriasis,[7] and compared tazarotene with it in plaque psoriasis.[5]

A report on congenital alopecia areata described treatments including minoxidil and a range of topical steroids, including fluocinonide.[4] On forums, one user with alopecia barbae reports being given fluocinonide with Protopic and seeing no change after three weeks;[14] another reports it flared after cycling off it while clobetasol worked.[13]
Topical fluocinonide is used in oral lichen planus and oral vesiculoerosive diseases, with topical corticosteroids described as the mainstay.[3][6][9][2]
Skin atrophy is the common potential adverse effect.[1] Tachyphylaxis was studied in a 1983 trial.[8] Wikipedia also notes cortisol suppression in veterinary use after a week of exposure.[1]

Clinical trials include the 2025 oral lichen planus RCT (47 patients),[6] a Cochrane review that covered corticosteroids in discoid lupus,[12] older randomized comparisons with betamethasone valerate,[10][11] a psoriasis phototherapy trial,[7] and a trial in oral vesiculoerosive disease.[9]

timeline.event: Double-blind trial comparing fluocinonide and betamethasone valerate published.[10]
Letter on topical fluocinonide and tachyphylaxis published.[8]
Randomized trial in oral lichen planus published.[6]
